clips.text: Today's real skill isn't the bargaining phrases — it's knowing where they belong. Get that part right, and the rest is easy and even fun.
Esta le doy en quinientos.
A craft stall with no price tag, no cash register, no receipt — that's an invitation to negotiate. A supermarket or a chain store is not. Reading the room correctly comes first.
You're at an open craft stall, no price marked. Ask a friendly opening question. Speak now.
¿Cuál es su mejor precio?
Se lo dejo en cuatrocientos.
Now you make a counter-offer, friendly, not aggressive. This is a conversation, not a demand — smiling and showing genuine interest in the piece gets you further than pressure ever will.
Offer a lower price, warmly. Speak now.
¿Se lo puedo dejar en trescientos cincuenta?
A friendly back-and-forth like this commonly lands somewhere around thirty percent off the opening price — not a rule, just a rough shape of how these conversations tend to go.
Va, trato hecho.
And if the answer is a flat no, that's the end of it — pushing further is the one move that actually sours the exchange. Thank them and decide whether to buy at the stated price.
The vendor can't go any lower. Thank them warmly, whether or not you buy. Speak now.
Está bien, muchas gracias.
¿Cuál es su mejor precio? ¿Se lo puedo dejar en trescientos cincuenta? Está bien, muchas gracias.

I10 complete. First, read the room — craft stall or supermarket. If it's a stall, ¿cuál es su mejor precio? opens it, a friendly counter-offer moves it, and a warm gracias closes it either way, deal or no deal. Money doesn't need to be tense to be real.
A traveller bargains for a craft item at an open-air stall, then accepts the final price gracefully.
Esta le doy en quinientos.
¿Cuál es su mejor precio?
¿Se lo puedo dejar en trescientos cincuenta?
Va, trato hecho.
